slides: This opening frames the chapter as a single mechanism rather than a list of theorems. The instructor should emphasize that compact Kahler geometry supplies identities among operators, and those identities are what allow harmonic representatives to remember complex type and Lefschetz structure.

Use this slide as the table of contents for the lecture. The point is not to prove each result immediately, but to show how every named object in the chapter has a job in the argument: identities compare Laplacians, then Lefschetz organizes the resulting cohomology.

The generated concept route gives students a place to locate every theorem before formulas arrive. Ask them to trace the shortest path from a commutator identity to the Hodge decomposition statement, then ask which assumption would be lost on a merely Hermitian compact manifold.

Present the identities as a translation device. The formulas are often remembered as signs and constants, but the pedagogical point is stronger: the Kahler metric makes the Dolbeault differentials and Lefschetz lowering operator interact so tightly that adjoints become commutators.

This is the bridge from differential operators to topology. Stress that compactness gives Hodge theory, while the Kahler identities identify which Laplacian is being used. Without this comparison, a de Rham class need not have a harmonic representative that visibly decomposes by complex type.

This slide makes the decomposition visible in the familiar diamond layout, but the instructor should keep the logic analytic. The diamond is not an assumption. It is the readable display of harmonic representatives after the Laplacian comparison has made de Rham classes compatible with bidegree.

Move slowly through the string picture. The operator L raises degree by wedging with the Kahler form, while Lambda lowers and H records the weight. Primitive classes are not minor exceptions; they are the seeds from which the entire Lefschetz decomposition is rebuilt.

The finite checks are not offered as proofs of the theorems. They are a debugging environment for the same bookkeeping. When students see the commutator relations hold in a small exterior algebra model, the abstract Lefschetz decomposition becomes a controlled representation-theoretic pattern.

The Hodge index theorem is a good place to pause and prevent a misleading intuition. Kahler metrics produce positive norms on forms, but the intersection pairing has its own signature. The primitive decomposition tells us exactly where the signs live.

This lab is deliberately small enough to do live. Have students choose primitive inputs before they compute the raised classes. The failed raise is important because it turns primitive from a definition into an observable stopping condition inside a finite cohomology ledger.

Close by returning to the chapter thesis. The compact Kahler assumption is powerful because it aligns three languages: elliptic operators, complex bidegrees, and Lefschetz representation theory. That alignment is exactly what the next chapter packages as Hodge structures and polarisations.
